Heritage sites by state

Heritage sites in Himachal Pradesh: temples, forts, monasteries

By @archaeologywala for Talaash Heritage · Updated 15 October 2026

Himachal Pradesh has two UNESCO listings: the Great Himalayan National Park (2014) and the Kalka-Shimla Railway, part of the Mountain Railways of India (2008). Its other heritage includes the Masrur rock-cut temples, Kangra Fort, Baijnath, the stone and wooden temples of Chamba and Bharmour, Tabo Monastery in Spiti and colonial Shimla.

We design heritage study tours of Kangra, Chamba, Shimla and Spiti for groups on request.

Why Himachal's heritage is worth a closer look

Himachal is usually sold as a hill holiday, but its valleys hold a long history of small kingdoms, trade routes and religious centres. Hill states such as Kangra, Chamba, Kullu, Mandi, Bushahr and Guler kept their own courts for centuries, some until 1947. Their patronage produced temples in stone and in timber, carved wooden palaces and the Pahari schools of miniature painting. In Lahaul, Spiti and Kinnaur, Buddhist monasteries connect Himachal with the Tibetan world.

The state also has a colonial layer. Shimla became the summer capital of British India from 1864, and its churches, offices and the Viceregal Lodge are part of that story; see our heritage walk in Shimla guide.

Museums in Himachal Pradesh

  • Bhuri Singh Museum, Chamba. Pahari paintings, Chamba rumals and inscribed fountain slabs.
  • Himachal State Museum, Shimla. Sculpture, painting and crafts from across the state.
  • Kangra Art Museum, Dharamshala. Kangra paintings, textiles and objects.

UNESCO World Heritage Sites in Himachal Pradesh

The Great Himalayan National Park, in Kullu district, was inscribed in 2014 as a natural site for its high-altitude forests, meadows and species. The Kalka-Shimla Railway (opened 1903) was added in 2008 to the Mountain Railways of India listing, alongside the Darjeeling and Nilgiri railways. Its narrow-gauge line climbs through many tunnels and over arched bridges, and the stations are part of the heritage.

For the full national list, including the serial sites, see UNESCO World Heritage Sites in India.

Ancient temples in Himachal Pradesh

The Masrur temples in Kangra district are a group of monolithic shrines cut from a sandstone ridge, usually dated to around the 8th century. They were planned in the Nagara style and left partly unfinished, and an earthquake in 1905 damaged them. Masrur is one of the few rock-cut temple complexes in north India and a good companion to our session on rock-cut sacred architecture.

Baijnath, near Palampur, is a Shiva temple with inscriptions of 1204 that record its building by local merchants. Chamba has the Lakshmi Narayan group of stone temples and the Hari Rai temple, and Bharmour, the old capital, has the Lakshana Devi temple with a carved wooden facade and a bronze image whose inscription names the 7th to 8th-century king Meruvarman. In Kullu and Mandi, the Hidimba temple at Manali (1553) shows the pagoda-like timber roof style, and Mandi's Bhutnath and Panchvaktra temples stand by the Beas. Our Nagara temple architecture session helps you read both the stone and timber forms.

Forts, palaces and monasteries

Kangra Fort, above the meeting of two rivers, is one of the oldest forts in the Himalayan foothills. It was held by the Katoch rulers, taken by the Mughals under Jahangir in 1620, and later by the Sikhs and the British. The 1905 earthquake damaged it badly. Naggar Castle in Kullu, a timber and stone palace, and Kamru Fort in Kinnaur show the local building tradition called kath-kuni, alternate courses of wood and stone that resist earthquakes.

Tabo Monastery in Spiti was founded in 996 CE by the translator Rinchen Zangpo and still has its original mud-built halls with early murals and clay sculptures. Key, Dhankar and Lhalung are other important Spiti monasteries. Tabo's art is fragile: no flash and no touching the walls. McLeodganj, above Dharamshala, is the seat of the Tibetan government-in-exile and holds the Tsuglagkhang complex.

Archaeology in the hills

Himachal's archaeology is less known than its temples but is worth noting. Stone tools of the Lower Palaeolithic have been reported from river terraces in the Beas, Banganga and Sirsa valleys, part of what archaeologists call the Sohanian tradition of the north-western foothills. Our stone tools up close workshop shows students how such tools were made and classified.

The historic period is known from inscriptions and coins as much as from buildings. Coins of the Kuninda people, who ruled parts of the hills around the 2nd century BCE to 3rd century CE, have been found in the region. Copper plate grants of the Chamba rulers, many kept in the Bhuri Singh Museum, record land gifts and are the main source for the kingdom's early history. Inscribed fountain slabs (panihars) in Chamba district combine water supply, religious merit and royal commemoration.

The 1905 Kangra earthquake is a key event for anyone visiting. It destroyed or damaged Kangra Fort, Masrur, many temples and much of Dharamshala, so what you see at several sites is a ruin shaped by a single day. That makes the region useful for discussing how conservation decides what to restore and what to leave.

Living heritage: painting, timber and fairs

The Pahari painting schools of Guler, Kangra, Chamba and Basohli flourished from the 17th to 19th centuries and are a high point of Indian miniature painting. Chamba rumals, embroidered cloths, are a related craft. Kullu Dussehra, Mandi Shivratri and Minjar in Chamba are fairs where village deities are carried in procession, and they show how temples still organise community life in the hills; our talk on temples as social institutions explores this.

Kath-kuni building is itself living heritage, though concrete is replacing it fast. Groups interested in recording old houses can use the methods in our documentation workshop.

Planning a heritage trip in Himachal Pradesh

Kangra valley (Dharamshala, Kangra Fort, Masrur, Baijnath) and Chamba make a good five-day trip. Shimla can be reached by the heritage railway from Kalka. Spiti needs a separate, longer trip and is accessible mainly in summer; altitude matters for school groups. Roads can close in winter and the monsoon. Check the ASI or state website before you go.

Questions people ask

How many UNESCO sites are there in Himachal Pradesh?

Two listings include Himachal: the Great Himalayan National Park, inscribed in 2014, and the Kalka-Shimla Railway, which was added in 2008 to the Mountain Railways of India serial site.

What are the oldest temples in Himachal Pradesh?

The Masrur rock-cut temples, of about the 8th century, and the Lakshana Devi temple at Bharmour, associated with King Meruvarman of the 7th to 8th centuries, are among the oldest. Baijnath has inscriptions of 1204.

Why is Tabo Monastery important?

It was founded in 996 CE and still has its original halls, murals and clay sculptures, which makes it one of the oldest continuously working Buddhist monasteries in the Himalaya and a key site for early Tibetan Buddhist art.

Can Talaash Heritage arrange a heritage trip to Himachal?

Yes, on request. We design study tours for schools, colleges and adult groups, for example Kangra valley with Masrur and Baijnath, or Chamba, and can add a lecture on temple architecture before you travel.
